thread.title: Tech Today: Chips Sink, Apple Shifts iPhone Plans, Amazon’s in Prime Time

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Tech Today: Chips Sink, Apple Shifts iPhone Plans, Amazon’s in Prime Time
text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated April 19, 2018 11:25 a.m. ET Here are some things going on today in the world of tech :
Taiwan Semi spooks chip stocks
There are a couple of ugly developments causing pain for chip stocks this morning.
One is the report this morning by contract chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ) of Q1 revenue of $8.46 billion, missing the Street’s average estimate for $8.53 billion. The company cited some “softness” in mobile products, likely a reference to what has been cited for months now as a breakdown in the smartphone market.
The forecast was also weaker. Taiwan Semi shares are lower by $2.23, or over 5%, at $39.69.
Remember this comes after the weakness yesterday in stocks of chip equipment makers ASML ( ASML ) and Lam Research ( LRCX ). Their shares are weak again today.
Susquehanna Financial ’s Mehdi Hosseini writes that the soggy report reflects " steeper than expected inventory digestion by premium Smart Phone customers, particularly Apple.” He notes that Apple ( AAPL ) is "is aggressively clearing inventories” of the “A11” processors for its iPhone , "as it prepares” for the new model of iPhone this fall, presumably using a newly designed “A12” chip.
Qualcomm runs aground in China
The other thing spooking the market this morning is Qualcomm ( QCOM ) announcing this morning it has been forced to refile its application to acquire NXP Semiconductors ( NXPI ) with China ’s regulators, MOFCOM . Qualcomm’s been trying for over a year to close the deal, and sounded quite confident last month it would be able to do so, with China being the last regulatory hurdle.
Qualcomm’s agreement with NXP has been extended now to July 25th. There's a $2 billion break-up fee Qualcomm has to pay NXP if they have to back out of this.
Qualcomm shares are down $2.35, or 4%, at $52.88, while NXP is down $4.60, or 4%, at $108.39.
Whither iPhone?
What does the TSM report mean for the iPhone?
Raymond James chip analyst Christopher Case writes that “we are seeing a troubling trend at Apple as rising component costs necessitate higher prices, and consumers’ price elasticity at the high end doesn’t seem to be as strong as Apple had expected."
As a result, he thinks Apple is now planning to make 50% of this fall’s iPhone shipments using cheaper LCD screens rather than the OLED screens that debuted on the iPhone X.
“Changes surrounding build plans have driven increased uncertainty in the supply chain,” he concludes. He urges investors to use the uncertainty to buy shares of Qorvo ( QRVO ), the wireless chip maker whose parts are found in some iPhone models.
Apple shares are down $3.90, or 2%, at $173.94, while Qorvo shares are down $1.83, or 2.5%, at $71.29.
But wait, Nvidia!
Evercore ISI ’s C.J. Muse finds a silver lining in all this: He notes Taiwan Semi is "confident on longer-term 'mega-trends' such as HPC, 5G, and AI.”
"Here, the company suggested that AI will boost the attach rate of accelerators in the data center,” and because of that, Muse recommends shares of his “top pick,” Nvidia ( NVDA ). Nvidia shares this morning are down $6.87, or 3%, at $229.50.
Amazon an island of calm
You know who’s not affected by all this chip stuff is Amazon ( AMZN ), which announced yesterday in its annual letter from CEO Jeff Bezos that it now has 100 million people using its Prime membership service. Amazon shares are up $32.39, or 2%, at $1,560.23.
Aegis Capital ’s Victor Anthony writes that this is 10 million more than he had estimated, and is a "material positive for the business given that Prime members, per most estimates we have seen, spend almost double that of a non-Prime member on an annual basis."
He thinks the Primes spend $1,300 annual on average, versus just $700 for most Amazon shoppers. He also thinks they "shop on Amazon 25x per year versus 14x for non-Prime members."
Macquarie Research ’s Ben Schachter dissects the language of the letter, pointing out that Bezos frames the company’s top priorities in order of importance: "Prime, AWS, 3P Marketplace, Alexa, Amazon devices.” One takeaway is that “Alexa,” Amazon’s voice-driven assistant software, is given its own category.
"AMZN is clearly aiming to establish Alexa as its own ecosystem," he writes.
Roku bounces back
That focus on Alexa comes after Amazon yesterday struck a deal with Best Buy ( BBY ) to sell television sets with Alexa software built in.
You might think that would threaten smart TV technology maker Roku ( ROKU ), but actually, its shares are up $1.25, or 4%, at $32.97.
Needham & Co .’s Laura Martin , who has a Buy rating on the shares, and a $50 price target. She’s unfazed, noting that Roku’s code is already on 150 different TV models, versus just 10 outlined by Amazon and Best Buy.
Moreover, the Best Buy deal "eliminates AMZN as a competitive threat in Wal Mart, Costco, Target, etc, and Best Buy can still sell all other Roku TVs."
She also notes that one of the brands Amazon is partnering with, Insignia , “hasn’t been in the top 13 TVs for the past 10 years, while Roku’s TVs have added 1,200 basis points of market share."
